The paper presents an adaptation of Greenberg's potential flow model to predict the aerodynamic loads on a vertical-axis wind turbine blade.
The model is extended to handle multi-harmonic oscillations in effective angle of attack and incoming flow velocity, which are more representative of the blade kinematics at low tip-speed ratios.
The experimental data is from a scaled-down single-bladed H-type Darrieus wind turbine with a NACA0018 airfoil profile, chord length of 6 cm, and span of 15 cm.
The experiments were conducted at a Reynolds number of 50,000 based on the blade rotational velocity of 0.89 Hz.

For low tip-speed ratios (λ=1.5), the Greenberg model predicts the maximum radial force coefficient well, but deviates from the experimental results once the effective angle of attack exceeds the critical stall angle of 13.1°.

For higher tip-speed ratios (λ=4.5), the Greenberg model predicts the maximum radial load coefficient and its timing well, but underestimates the magnitude during the downwind portion of the cycle due to blade-wake interactions.

The paper states that the proposed application of the Greenberg model to vertical-axis wind turbine kinematics shows great potential to diagnose regions of separated flow and quantify the relative influences of dynamic stall and turbine kinematics on the blade loading.

The authors note that future research can readily extend this method to any airfoil undergoing an arbitrary combination of pitching, surging and heaving, following a kinematic profile which can be approximated by a Fourier series.
